title: How to sell Tennr
lede: Tennr reads the faxed referrals that pile up at healthcare providers and turns them into patients ready to be seen. Its best buyers are family-run equipment suppliers, and a surprising number of the ones that look family-run have already been bought.

company.name: Tennr
company.one_liner: Tennr automates referral intake: it reads faxed orders, chases missing paperwork, checks eligibility and payer rules, and starts prior authorizations.

glossary.ICP: Ideal customer profile: the kind of company that buys, and why. It describes a company, not a person.
glossary.persona: A role inside the ICP company: what they own and why they would care.
glossary.buying signal: Something you can see from outside that makes the pain urgent now, not just news.
glossary.roll-up: A company that grows by buying many smaller ones. Buying decisions move to its head office.
glossary.DME: Durable medical equipment: CPAP machines, oxygen, ventilators, wheelchairs and the supplies that go with them.
glossary.CGM: Continuous glucose monitor: a wearable sensor for diabetes, supplied and billed monthly.
glossary.prior authorization: Approval an insurer must give before it will pay for the equipment.
glossary.competitive bidding: Medicare's program where suppliers bid for the right to serve an area or product line at a set price.
glossary.intake: Everything between a referral arriving and the patient being ready to receive equipment: reading the order, checking insurance, collecting paperwork.

lessons.title: Who buys this?
lessons.idea: The intake coordinator uses Tennr all day. The owner signs, because the saving shows up as people they no longer have to hire.

blocks.heading: The decision
blocks.body: Tennr lists six kinds of customer [s1]. By our count, 11 of its 21 customer stories are home medical equipment, sleep or supply companies [s2]. That is where the proof is, so that is the {{ICP}}.

items.label: Industry
items.value: Home medical equipment ({{DME}}) suppliers: sleep, respiratory and diabetes ({{CGM}}) [s3]

items.label: Size
items.value: 2 to 40 locations. A small {{intake}} team working hundreds of faxes a day [s4, s5]

items.label: Region
items.value: Anywhere in the US: the paperwork follows Medicare and insurer rules, not geography

items.label: Ownership
items.value: Independent, family or regionally owned, so the decision is made in the building

items.label: The pain, in their words
items.value: "I would have had to hire 3 to 4 more people to keep up with the volumes we were doing." (a customer's CEO) [s6]

items.label: Not a fit
items.value: Owned by a national chain, a public {{roll-up}}, a hospital or a private equity platform. Single stores. Cash retail. Existing customers

items.label: Why now
items.value: Medicare restarts {{competitive bidding}}: bid window targeted for late fall 2026, contracts from January 2028 [s7]

items.title: Owner, CEO or president
items.body: Owns the P&L. Cares because every growth spurt so far has meant hiring intake staff. CEOs speak for the customer in the Home Medix and Eastern MedTech stories [s6, s8].

items.title: Director of intake or operations manager
items.body: Owns the fax queue and the backlog. Your champion: they feel the pain daily [s5, s9].

items.title: Revenue cycle or reimbursement manager
items.body: Owns denials and audit-ready paperwork. Asks whether the documents will hold up [s10].

items.title: Intake coordinator
items.body: Keys faxes into the billing system. Turnover is high, which is part of the owner's pain [s10].

blocks.title: The segment you are not picking yet
blocks.body: Tennr is hiring a seller for health systems right now, and the job post talks about 6 to 12 month cycles and seven-figure deals [s11]. That is a real market, but not the one to learn on. Equipment suppliers already buy, and the owner can say yes in one meeting.

quiz.q: The intake coordinator at a 12-location sleep supplier loves your demo. Who most likely signs?
options: The intake coordinator
The owner or CEO
The referring physician
The IT contractor
quiz.why: In a family-run supplier the owner holds the budget, and the saving lands as hires they don't make. The coordinator is your best reference, not your signer.

lessons.title: Where are they?
lessons.idea: A list is only useful if every row is the company you think it is. In home medical equipment the usual mistake is ownership: the local name stays up long after a national buyer moves in.

blocks.caption: Every row: homepage fetched, ownership searched, something dated in the last 12 months, not a customer or competitor. Blank "why now" means no live signal this week, not a bad fit.

blocks.title: Bought five months ago
blocks.body: Dynamic Healthcare Services, four locations in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, fits the card on every line. A national provider bought it on 29 April 2026 [s31], and its site now says so [s32]. A list built in March would still have it as independent, so run the ownership check again every time you use a list.

blocks.title: "Family owned" on the homepage, private equity on the cap table
blocks.body: DASCO's homepage says it is a family owned company [s33]. A private equity firm recapitalized it in 2020 [s34] and still lists it as active [s35]. The about page is marketing, not a record.

blocks.title: The domain gave it away
blocks.body: Rochester Oxygen & CPAP still turns up in searches for local suppliers. Its domain answers with a redirect to a national roll-up's site [s36]. Opening the homepage settled it in one click.

blocks.title: An existing customer in a local search
blocks.body: Performance Home Medical came up in our search for independent respiratory suppliers in the Pacific Northwest. It is a Tennr customer [s5], and its site now lists a corporate office in Houston [s37]. Check every row against the customer page before you write.

blocks.title: Same name, three companies
blocks.body: Alpine Home Medical is a family-owned chain of 11 stores in Utah and Idaho [s23]. Alpine Medical is a separate family business in Cody, Wyoming [s38]. Domain plus city settles which one a story is about.

blocks.title: We dropped 24 good-looking suppliers
blocks.body: They fit on paper, but we couldn't prove who owns them or that they traded in the last 12 months. A "© 2026" footer proves nothing: many sites print the current year automatically. A shorter list you trust beats a longer one you don't.

blocks.heading: What the checks caught
rows: Owned by a national chain, roll-up, hospital or private equity firm
Dynamic Healthcare Services [s31], DASCO [s34], Rochester Oxygen & CPAP [s36], Roberts Home Medical [s39]

blocks.heading: Run these on your own list, in this order
items: Open the domain. Name, services and city must match what you wrote. A redirect or a parked page ends it.
If the name is common, search it with the city. Keep the row only when domain, city and industry all agree.
Search "<company> acquired" and "<company> parent company", then read the site footer. Don't trust "family owned" on its own.
Find something dated in the last 12 months: a job post, a news post, a new branch. A copyright year doesn't count.
Compare against the customer stories and the competitor list.
Count locations on the company's own site. Outside 2 to 40, drop it.
Can't settle a check? Drop the row.

quiz.q: Two suppliers on your list are both called "Alpine": 11 stores around Salt Lake City, and 4 around Cody, Wyoming. How do you know which one a news story is about?
options: Whichever has more locations
Match the story's domain and city to the row
Ask the owner on the first call
Keep both and let the reply sort it out
quiz.why: Name alone never settles a collision. Domain plus city does, and it takes a minute.

quiz.q: A supplier's homepage says "family owned since 1987". What do you still need?
options: Nothing, the site says it
An ownership search: "acquired", "parent company", recapitalization
Their number of employees
A reference from a customer
quiz.why: DASCO's homepage says family owned, and a private equity firm has owned a stake since 2020. Pages lag deals by years.

lessons.title: When are they ready?
lessons.idea: The same supplier is a bad target in March and a good one in September. A {{buying signal}} is something you can see from outside that makes the fax pile urgent now.

items.name: Hiring for intake or authorizations
items.watch: Job posts for authorization specialists, intake or order-entry staff, insurance verification
items.why: The {{prior authorization}} and order paperwork is growing faster than the team. The budget for the hire can pay for Tennr instead.

example.fact: Posted an Authorization Specialist covering 6 locations on 26 Aug 2026, then a multi-site care coordinator on 23 Sep [s13]

items.name: A new branch
items.watch: New locations on the site, or a new branch in Medicare's public supplier registry
items.why: More orders into the same intake team. Each branch adds referral sources and fax lines.

example.fact: Registered a new branch in Escanaba, MI on 27 Aug 2026 [s22] and posted an intake role there

items.name: A change in the revenue cycle team
items.watch: Job posts or announcements for reimbursement, billing or revenue cycle managers
items.why: A new manager reviews how documents flow in their first 90 days, and denials land on their desk.

example.fact: Posted an Assistant Reimbursement Manager on 12 Aug 2026 [s16]

items.name: A rule with a date on it
items.watch: Medicare competitive bidding milestones for the product lines they sell
items.why: Winning a contract means pricing tight and handling more volume. Losing one means cutting cost. Both point at intake.

example.company: Regional Home Care and Medical Comfort Systems
example.fact: Both sell CGMs. The bid window for Round 2028, which includes CGMs, is targeted for late fall 2026 [s7]

items.name: A new product line
items.watch: A supplier adding CGM, ventilation or sleep testing
items.why: One Tennr customer's CGM launch doubled its inbound documents in two months [s8].

example.fact: None of the accounts announced a new line inside 90 days. Watch for it.

blocks.title: Signals go stale
blocks.body: A job post is worth acting on for about 30 days, a new branch for about 60, a new manager for about 90. OxyCare Plus opened a branch in March 2026: six months on, that is history, not a reason to write.

quiz.q: Which of these is a buying signal for Tennr?
options: A supplier welcomes a new respiratory therapist to its clinical team (Aug 2026)
A supplier posts an authorization specialist job covering six branches (Aug 2026)
A supplier wins a local family-business award
quiz.why: Authorizations are the work Tennr does. A clinician hire [s18] or an award is news: nice to mention, but it doesn't make the fax pile urgent.

lessons.title: Who exactly?
lessons.idea: Reach the {{persona}} who owns the backlog first, then the one who signs. People change jobs all the time, so check someone still works there before you write.

rows: Head office, over the intake team
Job posts name the department (Total Respiratory's is called "Intake" [s21]); the company's employee list on professional networking sites, filtered by title
Head office; often a founding family
The About page of family businesses often names them; state business filings
Job posts for their team; Medicare's public supplier registry lists each branch's authorized official by title
Job posts describe their work: order entry, insurance checks, paperwork [s19]

blocks.heading: Check a person before you write
items: Their current job on their own profile names this company, and the company page links to this domain.
The title is current: a post, a job change or a company announcement from this year.
The location fits: someone at the Minnesota head office, not a branch driver three states away.
Still not sure? Write to the role through the company's contact page instead of guessing.

blocks.title: Otto can do this part
blocks.body: Otto finds people in each persona at your accounts and checks each one against their current employer before they go on a list. This course used public pages only, so it names no one.

blocks.title: Find one signer
blocks.body: Pick Corner Home Medical or Reliable Respiratory. Find the person who runs intake and the owner or CEO. For each, write down the evidence that they work there today.

lessons.title: What do you say?
lessons.idea: The first message is about them. It proves you looked, makes one point, and asks one question they can answer from memory.

left.label: The message everyone sends
left.body: Hi {first name}, hope you're well! I'm reaching out from Tennr, an AI-powered patient orchestration platform that helps DME providers streamline intake and unlock efficiency. Would you be open to a quick 15-minute call next week to explore how we could help Reliable Respiratory?

right.label: Yours
right.body:
Hi {first name}, saw Reliable Respiratory is hiring an authorization specialist to cover six locations, from Norwood up to Concord.

Usually that means prior auths and rental paperwork are growing faster than the team chasing them.

Are auths worked centrally in Norwood, or does each branch chase its own?
right.notes: Opens on their job post [s13], not on us. Names the pain the way they would. One either/or question. No meeting ask. 49 words.

items.title: Open on them
items.body: The signal from lesson 3, in their words: "authorization specialist", "six locations".

items.title: One sentence of why
items.body: From their side: the paperwork outgrowing the team. No product claims.

items.title: One easy question
items.body: Either/or, answerable in five words. Central or branch is also your first discovery question.

items.title: Under 90 words
items.body: No em dashes, no exclamation marks, no "hope you're well", no meeting ask.

quiz.q: Which opening line gets a reply from an intake director?
options: "I hope this finds you well!"
"Tennr processed over 10 million patients in 2025."
"Saw you're hiring three branch intake coordinators this month."
quiz.why: It proves you looked and is about their week. The second is true [s41] but it is about us.

lessons.title: Which Claude model for which job?
lessons.idea: Sorting accounts has a right answer, so you can measure it instead of guessing. We ran the same task on three models and scored them against our own checks.

blocks.takeaway: All three models caught all five real traps. Haiku's one miss was a boundary (2 locations is inside "2 to 40"), and its reasons claimed facts that weren't in the input, so read its reasons with care. Sonnet matched Opus for about 60% of the price here.

blocks.heading: What we'd use for each job in this course
rows: Sorting hundreds of accounts against the ICP
Haiku, with a human on the edges
14 of 15 at a fifth of Sonnet's cost. Its one miss was a boundary, so spot-check the rows near the limits
Researching an account, drafting first messages
15 of 15 here, specific reasons, about 60% of Opus's price
Deciding the ICP, a message to a key account, grading the agent's work
Also 15 of 15, with the clearest reasons. Few calls, so cost barely matters
blocks.caption: Prices used: Haiku 4.5 $1 / $5, Sonnet 5 $2 / $10, Opus 5.5 $4 / $20 per million input / output tokens [s42]. One run each, so treat small gaps as noise.

blocks.title: Effort is a second dial
blocks.body: Every current model also takes an effort setting, from low to max. A bigger model on low effort is sometimes a better trade than a smaller model.

quiz.q: You need to sort 2,000 suppliers into fit or no fit every month. Based on this lab, what do you do?
options: Opus on everything, to be safe
Haiku on everything, then a human checks the rows near the size and ownership limits
Skip the model and sort by hand
quiz.why: Haiku caught every real trap. Its one miss was an edge case, which is cheap for a person to check.

lessons.title: Can this run every week without me?
lessons.idea: Yes. An agent is a model with instructions, tools and a way to check its own work. Claude Managed Agents hosts it, runs it on a schedule, and a separate grader checks each run [s43].

steps.label: Agent
steps.detail: Tennr's ICP, the 5 signals and the message rules

steps.label: Tools
steps.detail: Web search and fetch (plus Otto if connected)

steps.label: Grader
steps.detail: Checks sources, dates and drafts against the rubric

steps.label: Report
steps.detail: New signals on the 23 accounts, each with a draft message

blocks.body:
cd agent
cp .env.example .env    # paste your Anthropic API key
bash launch.sh          # creates the agent on your schedule, runs once now
python3 report.py       # when the run finishes: download the report
blocks.caption: The kit is in `agent/`. The brief and account list are filled in from this course.

blocks.title: Cost and control
blocks.body:
Cost grows with the list: each run reads every account's site, careers page and news. We haven't measured it, so watch each run in the Console and keep the hard cap in `.env` (`RUN_BUDGET_CENTS`, 500 = $5).

The agent only writes a report and never sends anything.

blocks.title: Keep patient data out of it
blocks.body: Managed Agents is not currently covered by a HIPAA business associate agreement [s43]. This agent only reads public pages about companies. Don't give it referrals, faxes or anything about a patient.
To go further: connect Otto for verified people and Signal Agents that watch the same accounts as they change, or add a memory store so the agent never reports the same signal twice.

quiz.q: The first run flags a supplier that a national chain bought last month. What do you change so it doesn't happen again?
options: The schedule
The rubric: every account must pass an ownership check before a signal counts
Nothing, it's a one-off
quiz.why: The grader enforces the rubric on every run. Put the check there and it runs on every scheduled run, not just when you remember.

lessons.title: What happens next?
lessons.idea: A plan isn't pipeline. This course decided who to sell to and what to say. Sending, following up and handling replies happen over the next few weeks, and that is where it stops.

blocks.heading: Where this course stops
rows: Keeps the ICP and scores new accounts against it
Company search against the ICP, kept in a workbook
✓ once (lesson 3), then on your schedule with the agent (lesson 7)
Signal Agents watching the accounts continuously
Verified people and their current employer
A sequence for every account: first message and follow-ups
Campaigns on LinkedIn and email, paced within daily limits
Inbox triage and reply drafts for your approval
Reply rates per campaign, synced to a CRM without duplicates

blocks.heading: From this course to a campaign in Otto
items: **Accounts.** Import the 23 accounts from lesson 2 into a workbook called "Tennr course", with their domains, so Otto matches companies instead of creating duplicates.

**People.** Add the intake and operations leaders you find at each one (lesson 4). Run the import as a dry run first: every person should attach to one of your accounts, with no new companies created.
**Sequence.** Create a draft campaign from a template, put the lesson 5 message in as step 1, and add one or two follow-ups that bring a different finding instead of repeating the first message.
**Enrol and schedule.** Add the workbook, then set weekdays, a morning send window and a daily cap.
**Check.** Run the pre-launch check. It lists anything missing: copy, a connected mailbox or LinkedIn account, a schedule.
**Launch it yourself** when the copy reads right. Replies land in Otto's inbox, sorted by intent, with drafts for you to approve.

blocks.title: Nothing here sends on its own
blocks.body:
This course was built on public web data, without Otto connected, so no campaign was created. With Otto connected, the skill can set up steps 1 to 5 as a **draft** when you ask, and launching stays your decision.

Start at [otto-pilot.io](https://otto-pilot.io).

quiz.q: You import your contacts and the preview says it will create 18 new companies. What do you do?
options: Import anyway, the duplicates can be merged later
Fix the company names or domains so each person matches one of your accounts, then import
Skip the people and enrol the companies only
quiz.why: New companies mean your people won't attach to the checked accounts, so the campaign, signals and replies would all hang off duplicates. Fix the match first.

quiz.q: The pre-launch check says no mailbox that can see replies is connected. What happens if you press launch?
options: It sends, and replies are lost
It refuses to launch until the blocker is fixed
It sends LinkedIn steps only
quiz.why: Launch runs the same checks and won't start with a blocker, so you can't start a campaign that can't hear back.
